statement: To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.
heath_proof: Let there be set out two rational straight lines A, B commensurable in square only and such that the square on A, being the greater, is greater than the square on B the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A. [X. 29] And let the square on C be equal to the rectangle A, B. Now the rectangle A, B is medial; [X. 21] therefore the square on C is also medial; therefore C is also medial. [X. 21] Let the rectangle C, D be equal to the square on B. Now the square on B is rational; therefore the rectangle C, D is also rational. And since, as A is to B, so is the rectangle A, B to the square on B, while the square on C is equal to the rectangle A, B, and the rectangle C, D is equal to the square on B, therefore, as A is to B, so is the square on C to the rectangle C, D. But, as the square on C is to the rectangle C, D, so is C to D; therefore also, as A is to B, so is C to D. But A is commensurable with B in square only; therefore C is also commensurable with D in square only. [X. 11] And C is medial; therefore D is also medial. [X. 23, addition] And since, as A is to B, so is C to D, and the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable with A, therefore also the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable with C. [X. 14] Therefore two medial straight lines C, D, commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle, have been found, and the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C. Similarly also it can be proved that the square on C exceeds the square on D by the square on a straight line incommensurable with C, when the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line incommensurable with A. [X. 30]

**Statement:** To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.

**Step 1.** Let two rational straight lines A, B, commensurable in square only, be set out such that A is the greater and the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A [10.29].

**Step 2.** Let the square on C be equal to the rectangle A, B [2.14]. Since A, B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle A, B is irrational and the side of the square equal to it is irrational and is called medial [10.21]. Therefore C is medial.

**Step 3.** To the straight line C let there be applied, in a right angle, a parallelogram equal to the square on B [1.44] (the square on B being divided by its diameter into two triangles, which are applied to C in succession); being right-angled, it is a rectangle contained by C and its other side. Let that other side be D, so that the rectangle C, D is equal to the square on B.

**Step 4.** B is rational; therefore the square on B is rational [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. And the rectangle C, D is equal to the square on B; therefore the rectangle C, D is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** The rectangle A, B and the square on B, that is, the rectangle B, B, are parallelograms of the same height B; therefore as the rectangle A, B is to the square on B, so is A to B [6.1].

**Step 6.** The rectangle A, B is equal to the square on C, and the square on B is equal to the rectangle C, D; equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same, and the same has the same ratio to equal magnitudes [5.7]; therefore as the square on C is to the rectangle C, D, so is A to B [5.11].

**Step 7.** The square on C and the rectangle C, D are parallelograms of the same height C; therefore as the square on C is to the rectangle C, D, so is C to D [6.1]. Therefore as A is to B, so is C to D [5.11].

**Step 8.** Since A is greater than B and as A is to B, so is C to D, C is greater than D [5.14].

**Step 9.** Since A, B are commensurable in square only, A is incommensurable in length with B. And as A is to B, so is C to D; therefore C is incommensurable in length with D [10.11].

**Step 10.** Since A, B, C, D are four proportional straight lines, and the squares on them are similar figures similarly described upon them, as the square on A is to the square on B, so is the square on C to the square on D [6.22]. But the square on A is commensurable with the square on B, since A, B are commensurable in square; therefore the square on C is commensurable with the square on D [10.11]; that is, C, D are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. With Step 9, C, D are therefore commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** C is medial (Step 2), and D is commensurable in square with C (Step 10); but a straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial [10.23]. Therefore D is medial.

**Step 12.** Since A, B, C, D are proportional, and the square on A, the greater, is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A (Step 1), the square on C, the greater (Step 8), is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C [10.14].

**Step 13.** Therefore C, D are two medial straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 10, 11), containing the rational rectangle C, D (Step 4), and such that the square on the greater, C, is greater than the square on the less, D, by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C (Step 12); which was to be found.
